title: How the world changes over time
lead: Sudden, gradual, incremental, and recurring changes are different time patterns—not different input features.
bullets: Sudden: the old regime switches abruptly.
Gradual: old and new regimes coexist during a transition.
Incremental / recurring: intermediate change differs from a returning regime.
Blips: isolated noise is not necessarily a lasting regime change.
example: Bank illustrations: a pricing change can be sudden; staggered adoption gradual; evolving habits incremental; seasonal activity recurring.
takeaway: First ask how change unfolds over time. Then ask what changed: input data, outcome relationships, or data validity.

title: Monitoring: observe more than model accuracy
lead: Inputs, system execution, predictions, and business actions need different evidence.
bullets: Inputs: are the right records available and meaningful?
System: did the pipeline complete correctly and on time?
Model: are predictions useful on the current population?
Business: are permitted actions and outcomes being tracked?
example: A healthy churn job can still use a shifted population. A useful score can still lead to an inappropriate contact.
takeaway: Observability connects evidence to investigation; dashboards alone do not decide the remedy.

title: Monitoring architecture: from signal to response
lead: Collect linked evidence and route it to an owner who can investigate and act.
bullets: Signals: input, execution, and predictive evidence arrive at different times.
Context: link observations to run, feature, model, and cohort identity.
Routing: an alert has a defined recipient and response policy.
Authority: investigation and release approval remain separate.
example: A CRM missingness alert links to B017 and reaches source / operations owners; it does not promote M2.
takeaway: A useful monitoring design connects evidence, ownership, and a controlled response.

title: Data drift: a different customer mix
lead: Compare the same input definition across a reference cohort and the current cohort.
bullets: What changes: the distribution of valid model inputs.
Bank example: a campaign attracts more low-activity customers.
Available now: compare inputs without waiting for churn labels.
Limit: a changed distribution alone does not prove lost accuracy.
example: Both diagrams count 100 fictional customers using the same seven-day login bins. Only the customer mix changes.
takeaway: Choose a meaningful reference, comparable cohorts, and a defined response.

title: Concept drift: a different relationship
lead: The same inputs can have different outcomes while the deployed model keeps its earlier boundary.
bullets: What changes: churn risk given the same valid input information.
Bank example: new fees make active customers leave more often.
Evidence: link predictions to mature, reliable churn outcomes.
Model status: M1 stays fixed until a separately evaluated release changes it.
example: The two panels use the same 15 fictional feature positions. After the hypothetical change, some previously staying customers churn.
takeaway: A missing field is not concept drift; a statistical alarm is not a retraining approval.

title: Concept drift: how M1 starts making errors
lead: A fixed model can miss churners because the world changed—not because its software stopped running.
bullets: Inputs stay fixed: the two cohorts use identical feature positions.
M1 stays fixed: its earlier decision boundary is unchanged.
Outcomes change: a different relationship creates missed churners.
Evidence: the example uses mature labels, not outcomes already known on scoring day.
example: C1 has 5 logins and 5 products; C2 has 11 logins and 1 product. The same inputs now accompany different observed churn outcomes.
takeaway: Changed labels reveal the mismatch. Investigate causes, evaluate candidates, and use controlled release rather than automatic promotion.

title: Input checks now; quality checks later
lead: The target window creates a delay between a prediction and complete outcome evidence.
bullets: At scoring time: check freshness, missingness, execution, and coverage.
During the window: the full churn outcome is still unknown.
After ingestion: join labels to the original score and target window.
Evaluate by cohort: precision, recall, and calibration answer different questions.
example: Ana’s D0 score is saved with its context. Complete next-30-day evaluation must wait for that window and ingestion.
takeaway: An absent label does not mean the customer stayed.

title: Drift detection: methods and their purpose
lead: Methods compare inputs; they do not directly measure business value or model correctness.
bullets: Reference: name the population, period, and feature definition.
Thresholds: calibrate for the application rather than copying a universal rule.
Segments: inspect affected cohorts instead of relying only on an aggregate.
Action: investigate drift alongside quality, change, and business evidence.
example: Compare the same seven-day login feature before and after a campaign; investigate why the cohort mix changed.
takeaway: Interpret the signal alongside data validity, sample size, and downstream quality.

title: Data-quality faults and training-serving skew
lead: Invalid data and inconsistent preparation differ from a shifted valid population.
bullets: Data-quality fault: missing, stale, corrupt, or incompatible records.
Skew: training and production prepare the feature differently.
Inspect: definitions, cutoffs, joins, source changes, and code versions.
Repair the cause: retraining on defective inputs can preserve the defect.
example: A missing engagement field after CRM migration is invalid input. A 30-day production count replacing seven days is skew.
takeaway: Do not use the word “drift” as a diagnosis for every alarm.

title: A publication gate contains a bad batch
lead: The CRM incident illustrates a concrete input fault and a controlled response.
bullets: Detect: invalid records violate the agreed input contract.
Contain: hold the entire B017 batch before publication.
Investigate: relate cohort, source change, feature definition, and execution.
Keep M1: a source fault does not itself justify a new learned model.
example: Ana’s engagement value is missing, not zero. No new score or completed customer contact is invented.
takeaway: A gate blocks unsafe use; an alert sends evidence to someone who can investigate.

title: Respond: investigate, contain, repair, verify
lead: A monitoring signal opens a decision process; it does not select or approve a remedy.
bullets: Diagnose before choosing repair, rollback, fallback, or training.
Preserve evidence and the identity of failed attempts.
Validate the complete path after the chosen repair.
Request a model change only when evidence supports one.
example: Repair the CRM path, validate a new execution B017-R1, and retain M1 unless a separate model change is justified.
takeaway: Handoff to Luca: which dependencies made this failure possible?
